column1: A junior dev says: "MediaPlayer COULD have been written as MediaPlayer extends PlayState instead of holding an IState field — same end result, just inheritance instead of composition." What's the concrete problem with this suggestion, given MediaPlayer needs to represent playing, paused, AND stopped states over its lifetime?,"A single class can only extend ONE class in Java — if MediaPlayer extends PlayState, it could never also ""be"" PauseState or StopState at different points in time
column2: composition lets MediaPlayer swap which state object its state field points to at runtime, something inheritance to a single fixed parent can never do",This would only be a problem if IState were a class instead of an interface,There's no real problem — MediaPlayer extends PlayState would work identically,PlayState would need to be declared final to prevent this from working,,1,"This is the core reason composition was chosen for State: the ability to change what's referenced at runtime, which fixed single inheritance cannot offer.",1

column1: This is one of the sharpest reasons composition is often preferred over inheritance: with inheritance, a subclass's constructor is FORCED to run its parent's constructor first (super(), explicit or implicit) — you cannot skip it. With composition, when does the held object actually get constructed?,The held object is constructed automatically by the JVM the first time the field is declared,"Whenever the containing class's code chooses to construct it — DocumentProxy deliberately delays constructing RealDocument until display() is called, something impossible if DocumentProxy had inherited from RealDocument instead, since parent constructors always run immediately during subclass construction","Composition also forces immediate construction, identical to inheritance",There's no timing difference between the two approaches,,2,Composition gives full control over WHEN (or even whether) the held object gets constructed — a freedom inheritance's mandatory super() call does not offer.,1

column1: This tradeoff has a name worth knowing: with inheritance, a subclass inherits its parent's ENTIRE public interface automatically, whether it wants all of it or not. With composition, the containing class only exposes exactly what it chooses to manually delegate. Given RewardDecorator only needs IPayment's single pay() method (not a hypothetical User's ten methods), why might this "must manually delegate everything you want to expose" property of composition actually be a GOOD thing here rather than a downside?,It's never a good thing — composition should be avoided whenever inheritance is available,It only matters if the parent class has private fields,"It prevents RewardDecorator from accidentally inheriting and exposing methods it has no business exposing — since IPayment only has one method (pay()) anyway, there's nothing extra to accidentally leak, but in general, composition lets a class expose a deliberately narrow, curated interface instead of automatically inheriting everything a parent class happens to have, public or not",This property is unique to IPayment and doesn't generalize to other interfaces,,3,"Deliberate, narrow exposure is a genuine advantage of composition — it prevents unintentionally leaking a large inherited API surface.",1

column1: Pull together MediaPlayer (composition: IState state swappable at runtime) and BeverageMaker (inheritance: fixed permanent specialization). State the general rule for choosing between the two, in a way that would help decide correctly on a brand-new problem neither has been discussed yet.,The choice between them has no practical consequence and can be made arbitrarily,Always default to inheritance since it requires less code to write initially,Always default to composition since inheritance is universally considered a mistake in every case,"Reach for inheritance when a set of variants share a fixed, permanent structure and only specialize a small, unchanging part of it once at construction (like Espresso always being an Espresso and always following the same beverage-making steps)
column2: reach for composition when the varying behavior needs to change dynamically over the object's lifetime, when multiple unrelated behaviors need to be combined in one object, or when you want to keep the containing class's exposed API deliberately narrow rather than inheriting an entire parent's public surface",,4,"This is the synthesis rule tying the whole quiz together: permanent, fixed specialization suits inheritance, while dynamic, swappable, or narrowly-exposed behavior suits composition.",3
